item.title: Why Does It Bother Us So Much When Someone Doesn’t Like Us?
item.description:
Social Life

Why Does It Bother Us So Much When Someone Doesn’t Like Us?

Sometimes we're not trying to be liked. We're trying to feel safe.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • For those of us who grew up with rejection, disapproval can feel a lot bigger than it actually is.
  • Childhood rejection can teach us to mistake other people’s disapproval for danger, making us feel unsafe.
  • Learning to recognize the reason behind this fear can help you recognize that you will still be okay.

“I worry they don’t like me,” I said. I had been telling my therapist about a recent situation with someone in my social circle, a peer I had been trying to connect with but kept feeling like I was failing to win over.

“Can I point something out?” my therapist asked. She said it in that particular way therapists do when they are about to tell you something you probably aren’t going to love hearing.

“Yes,” I said weakly. Uh oh, I thought internally.

“I notice that you are very concerned with whether or not other people like you,” she said in her matter-of-fact way.

“Oh,” I said. Not sure whether I was feeling seen or exposed.

Source: Image by Jamie Hines from Pixabay

Why does it bother us so much when we learn someone doesn't like us?

My therapist was right. I do get really bothered when I think someone doesn't like me. Even when it's someone who, if I'm being completely honest, I don't particularly like myself.

If I were to think back, I would see a pattern of being so worried when people didn't like me. I remember college days, sitting up late in my dorm with my roommate, going over interactions with peers, worried that I was not liked. That's part of being young, you might think. And you might be right.

But I didn't grow out of it. I am in my late 30s and I still do this. A classmate made an offhand comment to me the other day in reference to a mutual peer. “I don't think they like you that much.” They probably meant it as nothing more than a passing observation in the middle of a conversation. But the moment they said it, I stopped listening to everything else. What do you mean? Why don't they like me? What did I do? Did I say something? My brain immediately went to work.

The friend who made the comment could tell I was spiraling. “Don't worry about it,” they said. “I think that's just how they are, they don't like some people.” But I couldn't let it go. I went home and asked my partner, “Do you think there is something I could have done?” Then I started combing through old text messages. I reread conversations, looking for anything that could possibly be interpreted the wrong way. Had I said something offensive? I searched for tone, I searched for evidence, for the moment when I might have said something that offended this person without realizing it.

“There are a couple things,” I said, showing my partner my phone. “What if they read this the wrong way?”

My partner finally took the phone out of my hands and—much to my satisfaction—snapped it shut. (I have one of those Android flip phones, so I still get to experience the small, deeply satisfying pleasure of dramatically slamming a phone closed like it's 2003).

article continues after advertisement

“Stop caring so much,” he said. “This shouldn't matter to you what they think. It doesn't change who you are. Just let it go.”

Except I couldn't. I thought about it for the rest of the day. And the strangest part was this: I didn't even particularly hold this person in such high regard. In fact, I find them a bit fake and superficial. So why did it matter so much that they didn't like me? Why can someone else's dislike feel so uncomfortable—even when we don't particularly like them either?

When rejection feels bigger than rejection

For many of us, the answer has less to do with the person who doesn't like us and much more to do with what their dislike represents.

If, like me, you grew up in an environment where rejection was common, you may have learned to pay very close attention to other people's reactions. We learned to listen for changes in someone's tone; to notice when someone seemed irritated, withdrawn, disappointed, or distant. You may have learned to constantly ask yourself whether they were mad at you, whether you had done something wrong, whether they were going to leave, or what you could do to make things better.

As a child, we depend on the adults around us for everything. Belonging and acceptance are deeply connected to our sense of safety1-2. But unlike adult relationships, we have no control over these relationships with our caregivers. We are at the mercy of their moods and their rejection or disapproval of us.

So when a child repeatedly experiences rejection or abandonment, they may begin to associate other people's disapproval with danger1-2. We learned that when someone is unhappy with me, I might not be safe.

This is why an adult's casual comment—“I don't think they really like you”—can sometimes feel wildly disproportionate to what actually happened. Logically, we might know that someone not liking us isn't a catastrophe. But our nervous system, which had to adapt to help us survive and stay safe, may not be so convinced.

Sometimes we're not trying to be liked. We're trying to feel safe.

The problem is that this strategy doesn't work particularly well in adulthood. We cannot control whether people like us. We cannot perfectly monitor every interaction and reread every text message until we find the exact sentence that caused someone to form an unfavorable opinion of us. And nor should we, because this is ridiculous. Because someone not liking us doesn't necessarily mean we've done anything wrong.

article continues after advertisement

We can be a good person and still be disliked.

So when you catch yourself spiraling over whether someone likes you, try to pause and ask yourself a question: Am I actually worried about this person's opinion of me—or am I worried about what their rejection might mean?

Sometimes, realizing that you're not actually afraid of being disliked helps you to understand what you are really afraid of: which is likely being rejected, being abandoned, or something else that signals to your brain that you are unsafe.

And once we understand that, we can respond to the wound instead of spending the rest of the day rereading our text messages. Because someone can dislike us and we can still be okay.

item.title: The Avoidance-Compound Trap: How Alcohol Compounds Stress
item.description:
Alcoholism

The Avoidance-Compound Trap: How Alcohol Compounds Stress

The relief alcohol may provide today can create more stress tomorrow.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • Alcohol may provide short-term stress relief but it leaves stressors unresolved.
  • Drinking to cope can impair your brain’s ability to recover from and adapt to future stress.
  • Relying on alcohol to manage stress eventually creates its own unique and ongoing stress.

If you've ever watched Grey's Anatomy, you know the scene. Whether it was a patient dying, a surgery going wrong, or someone's marriage falling apart, nearly every emotionally devastating episode ends with the main characters gathering at Joe's Bar, decompressing over a few drinks. The unspoken message comes through the screen loud and clear: “Alcohol helps decompress stress.”

Drinking to cope with stress has been a normalized practice in our culture, whether it’s in TV shows or in real life. In my own life, it was once my go-to response whenever I felt stressed by anything that happened in life. Whether it was an approaching deadline, an unexpected bill, an unpleasant argument, or even the dirty dishes piling up in the sink at the end of the day, my default was to reach for the bottle. “Thank goodness for the drink; I wouldn’t know how to handle all this stress if it wasn’t for it,” I’d think to myself.

The Stress-Drinking Loop
Source: Jeanette Hu | Sober Curiosity

Now, looking back, I wish I had known sooner that while a drink can help make the stress feel more manageable in the moment, over time, it can keep us stuck in what I have come to call the stress-drinking loop.

In this post, I want to share with you the triple compound effect alcohol can have on our lives and how it can keep us stuck in the avoidance-compound trap when drinking becomes our default response to stress.

Compound Effect #1: The Initial Stress

Here is the thing: a drink may be able to take the stress off our minds; it never removes the stressor from our lives. It simply allows us to avoid facing what stresses us out. When the effect of alcohol wears off the next morning, the dishes are still dirty, the bills are still unpaid, and the argument is still unresolved.

Making matters worse:

  • On top of the dirty dishes, there is now a hangover to nurse.
  • On top of the unpaid bills, there is now a new charge from last night's bar tab.
  • And on top of the original argument, there is now further damage to the relationship from the hurtful words after the third glass of wine.

When we drink to take the stressors off our minds, instead of disappearing, they tend to grow larger and larger like a snowball the morning after.

Compound Effect #2: The Compromised Ability to Cope With Stress

To make the bad news even worse, studies suggest that chronic alcohol consumption can impair our brain's ability to adapt to and recover from stressful experiences.

article continues after advertisement

In 2012, a group of researchers at the NIAAA (National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism) spent several weeks exposing laboratory mice to alcohol. Afterwards, they taught the mice that a particular tone predicted a mild foot shock. Before long, hearing the tone alone was enough to stress out the poor mice. The researchers then repeatedly played the same tone without delivering the shock, giving the mice a chance to learn that the danger had passed.

The control group—the mice that had not been exposed to alcohol—gradually realized they were safe and stopped becoming stressed at the sound of the tone. The alcohol-exposed mice, however, continued to experience a stress response (freezing) even after the threat had long passed.

In other words, not only does drinking do little to remove the sources of stress from our lives, but it may also interfere with our ability to recognize when a threat has passed.

Compound Effect #3: Drinking-Related Stress

Finally, when alcohol becomes the default response to the inevitable stress we face in everyday life, it often starts to create its own set of stress:

  • Health concerns from excessive consumption.
  • Relationship tension from concerned family members.
  • Compromised performance at work.

Not to mention the unique stress of managing cravings, the exhausting internal debate about whether to drink or not to drink, and the shame and self-loathing spiral the morning after. Those are the feelings I knew all too well towards the end of my drinking career. At some point, what started as a strategy to cope with stress had become, in itself, a major source of stress.

From the Avoidance-Compound Trap to the Stress-Drinking Loop

When we attempt to seek relief from the stress in our lives through drinking, we are simply delaying facing it through avoidance. While it offers us a temporary sense of relief, the unintended long-term result is that the stress accumulates and compounds, and we feel less and less equipped to cope with it.

article continues after advertisement

The avoidance-compound trap has kept me, and many clients I have worked with, in a stress-drinking loop, where a stressful event leads to the habitual response of drinking, and drinking, in turn, creates more stress that requires more drinking to cope. It creates a vicious cycle and keeps feeding into itself.

The First Step to Outgrow a Drinking Loop

Invisible Drinking Loop
Source: Jeanette Hu | Sober Curiosity

A stress-drinking loop is an invisible drinking loop that keeps a person stuck in the same unwanted drinking pattern. In an invisible drinking loop, drinking first starts as an attempt to solve another issue in our lives, and it often does work in the moment. But over time, it perpetuates the problem we drink to solve. For most regular drinkers, the stress-drinking loop is only one of the loops that keep their drinking pattern alive.

Because a drinking loop is rarely maintained by alcohol alone, breaking it often takes more than just stopping drinking. To truly outgrow a stress-drinking loop often asks us to change our relationship with stress. And that began with getting to know our stress responses and learning ways to tap into their power.

item.title: Imagining Synesthetically in Writing
item.description:
Cognition

Imagining Synesthetically in Writing

Cross-connecting senses can empower your imagination.

Posted August 23, 2026

Key points
  • Creative writers use sensory cues to help readers imagine what they have not experienced.
  • Zimbabwean author Yvonne Vera describes pain synesthetically, encouraging readers to cross-connect sensations.
  • Synesthetic descriptions engage readers cognitively, motivating them to imagine more intensely.

How do creative writers guide readers to imagine beyond their experiences? How can carefully chosen words make unimaginable pain imaginable? Zimbabwean author Yvonne Vera’s novel, The Stone Virgins (2002), describes a woman’s recovery after she is raped, mutilated, and forced to watch her sister’s murder during the violent conflicts of the early 1980s. To help readers sense what her character Nonceba is feeling, Vera cues them to cross-connect senses as synesthetes do.

Zimbabwean author Yvonne Vera in her garden in Bulawayo in 2004.
Source: Photo by Eric Beauchemin. Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0 International License.

Vera’s technique doesn’t require readers to be synesthetes. All people integrate sensorimotor information to produce unified, multimodal experiences, but synesthetes (about one in 40 to 100 people) experience some sensory qualities as connected, such as colors and musical tones (Ramachandran et al. 2020, 5). In the minds of synesthetes, these sensory cross-connections are conscious, systematic, idiosyncratic, and uncontrollable (Spence & Deroy 2013, 174-75). Having a vague feeling that the musical tone G should be green does not make one a synesthete. For a sound-to-color synesthete, G is automatically green, visually as well as auditorily.

To help readers imagine unfamiliar sensations, Yvonne Vera takes advantage of people’s tendency to compare information from different sensory channels. In some respects, all innovative writing is synesthetic. To describe a color so that a reader can feel it, an author needs to recruit senses beyond vision (Fitch 2020). Throughout The Stone Virgins, Vera offers multisensory cues to describe Nonceba’s experiences. She uses the same kind of multimodal prompts to open the mental world of Nonceba’s attacker, Sibaso, not so much to arouse sympathy as to show how the psychological damage caused by war can spread (Gagiano 2007, 64-70). The beauty of Vera’s language contrasts with the violence she describes (Norridge 2008, 170; McCann 2009, 85), but her synesthetic metaphors serve her story by opening both characters’ perspectives.

Examples of Cross-Sensory Metaphors in The Stone Virgins

Many of Vera’s cross-sensory cues involve visually perceived sounds or auditorily perceived sights. When Sibaso attacks Nonceba, she sees that his face is “so silent, I do not feel his first stroke. It falls on my flesh like light on water. Soundlessly. Like a sharp and burning light” (Vera 2002, 111). Vera describes Sibaso wandering through a battlefield, imaginatively mixing the last sights, sounds, and smells of the dead soldiers around him. Gazing at their bodies, he senses a “sight of thundering perfume” and “their last sounds, charred voices” (Vera 2002, 105). If Vera described Nonceba’s or Sibaso’s experiences with conventional sensory cues, readers might not appreciate the story of a woman whose lips are cut off and the traumatized man who cuts her. By choosing words that link senses in unusual ways, Vera helps readers remix and extend their memories so that they can sense inconceivable pain.

Sunglint on water, 20 June 2025.
Source: Stefan Brending/Creative Commons License CC-BY-SA-3.0 de.

Psychological studies of reading indicate that creative descriptions high in foregrounding (strikingly innovative language) catch readers’ attention and slow them down (Miall 2015, 17). In a study that asked participants to read stories and mark passages that gave them bodily feelings, the participants identified passages rich in foregrounding (Kuijpers and Miall 2011, 9). In a more recent study of readers’ imaginative experiences, investigators hypothesized that encountering “abstract and unique vocabulary may encourage deeper cognitive elaboration during reading, thus increasing the possibility of activating personally significant memories or associations” (Öncel et al. 2025, 96). These experimental findings and hypotheses align with literary theorist Viktor Shklovsky’s idea that great art breaks mental habits by reminding people how unfiltered perception feels (Shklovsky 2012, 22). Paradoxically, language that seems strange can make the sensations it evokes feel more immediate.

How Readers Respond to Synesthetic Prompts in Literature

Consciously or unconsciously, readers respond to fiction-writers’ verbal cues by reviving sensorimotor patterns triggered by semantic memory (Binder & Desai 2011, 527-31; Mannaert et al. 2019, 1201). When storytellers suspect that their readers have never felt anything like their characters’ experiences, they seek language that will inspire readers to mix and extend the sensorimotor patterns they can revive. Encouraging readers to think like synesthetes offers a kind of foregrounding likely to jolt readers out of their cognitive habits. A reader who pauses to reflect how a facial sensation “like light on water” might feel will work harder to imagine someone’s pain.

Innovative storytelling like Vera’s helps readers sense the emotional, personal aspects of pain that can be hard to describe (Norridge 2008, 159). In clinics, Vera’s synesthetic technique might help patients and health providers communicate about pain. The McGill Pain Questionnaire, which asks people if words such as “flickering” describe their pain, already has synesthetic tendencies (Melzack and Torgerson 1971, 52). The McGill terms, however, compare pain mainly to sensations in other somatosensory modalities such as touch, proprioception, and temperature detection.

If care providers are struggling to find the sources of patients’ pain, they might extend existing questionnaires by asking, “If your pain were a light, how would it look? If you could hear your pain, how would it sound? If your pain were an odor, how would it smell?” A cross-sensory comparison to neon light, grinding gears, or rotten eggs could lead to a communication breakthrough.
